issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: The negative appraisal items 'others can see what happened to me' and 'ashamed of what happened to my body' imply a trauma with visible bodily violation or injury, most classically interpersonal/sexual trauma, and are hard to reconcile with a generic man-made disaster trauma in the absence of any corroborating memory or trigger content about bodily injury or disfigurement.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Being Touched' is specifically linked to bodily violation/contact-based trauma and fits poorly with the rest of the profile for man-made disaster. The threat items center on environmental danger and escape planning, creating a cross-node mismatch with this touch-avoidance strategy.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: These items imply a trauma with prominent bodily violation or physical injury consequences. For a man-made disaster trauma, this specific body-focused pattern is not impossible, but in the absence of any supporting memory or trigger content and alongside the other items emphasizing generalized danger, it stands out as a hard-to-explain shift toward an assault/injury formulation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
issues.explanation: Within the current profile, avoidance of touch and bodily stress appears organized around bodily harm/shame, but the threat items are about environmental danger, escape planning, and unfamiliar places. That makes the strategy set only partially connected to the expressed threat/appraisal pattern.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: The profile is otherwise centered on persistent danger, vigilance, scanning, escape planning, and avoidance of unfamiliar places, which coheres with threat-focused beliefs after a man-made disaster. 'Failed Role' introduces a distinct self-evaluative theme that is not supported by the rest of the selected items and is hard to reconcile with this otherwise purely danger/safety formulation. Given the active formulation emphasizes Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies and Maladaptive Strategies → Threat, a danger-based appraisal would better fit the linked hypervigilance and checking strategies than a role-failure appraisal.

vignette:
Nisha Patel was 32 when she came for treatment, a first-term City Council member who had built a public identity around composure and accessibility. The event that changed that happened six months earlier at a crowded evening town hall in a municipal building downtown. She had stayed late after the formal meeting, speaking with residents in a narrow corridor outside the chamber, when an explosive device detonated near the entrance. She remembered the violent concussion more than a coherent sequence: the lights cutting out, plaster dust filling the air, the crush of bodies surging toward the exits, people screaming and falling over one another in the dark. What stayed with her most was the trapped feeling. For several seconds she could not tell where the nearest way out was, and as she was pushed against the wall she became certain that if there were a second blast she would die before she could get clear. Even now, enclosed public buildings, evening events, and any room where she cannot immediately locate a door carry that same charge.

In the weeks after, Nisha had come to believe that the bombing revealed something fundamental rather than exceptional: the world was dangerous, people could turn violent without warning, and safety depended on never letting her guard down. She was certain that what had happened proved how quickly ordinary civic life could become lethal. At night this conviction intensified. Darkness felt like reduced information, fewer cues, more opportunity for danger to approach unseen. She found herself thinking that she had to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, and that if she relaxed even briefly she would miss the sign that could save her.

Those beliefs began to organize her days. Before entering any council chamber, restaurant, constituent office, or campaign venue, she now identified exits and secondary exits before she could settle into her seat. If an event was in an unfamiliar building, she often declined it altogether, telling staff she had a scheduling conflict when in fact she could not bear the thought of being somewhere she had not already assessed for danger. During meetings she scanned faces in the audience, vigilant for dangerous people, and tracked hands, bags, and sudden movements instead of listening fully to whoever was speaking. She also started avoiding physical exertion: she stopped taking the stairs to council offices, cut short walks between buildings, and avoided rushing, because any pounding in her chest or shortness of breath made her feel exposed and less able to react. In her mind these habits were not excessive but necessary; if the world was this dangerous, being on guard all the time felt like the only rational way to move through it.

Over time, the habits that were meant to keep her safe made danger feel even closer. Because she was constantly checking the room, every public appearance produced something to notice: a man lingering near the back wall, an unfamiliar aide entering late, a door that seemed partially blocked, a sharp sound from the hallway. The fact that she always had to map an escape route before she felt comfortable meant she rarely felt comfortable at all. Avoiding unfamiliar places narrowed her world until even routine invitations felt risky by default. Nights became the worst; after evening council sessions she would sit awake in her apartment, listening for sounds in the corridor outside her door, unable to feel safe enough to sleep. The more she lived this way, the more convinced she became that her vigilance was justified. If she was this alert, she reasoned, it must be because there was truly so much to watch for.

This had begun to alter her work in visible ways. Staff noticed that she insisted on arriving early to every venue so she could inspect the layout and choose where to sit. She repositioned chairs in community rooms so she would not have her back to an entrance. She turned down site visits in unfamiliar neighborhoods unless she could be given detailed floor plans in advance. Constituents experienced her as distracted; during one listening session she realized she had spent more time monitoring a man in a heavy jacket near the door than hearing a resident describe a housing complaint. She was ashamed of this, but what frightened her most was the idea that lowering her guard would mean repeating the mistake she believed everyone had made before the blast-assuming normalcy where there was none.

By the time she sought help, she was exhausted from living as if threat were always about to break through. She still told herself that constant vigilance was the price of survival, yet her life had become smaller and more governed by exits, lighting, and familiar rooms. She came in after canceling an evening public forum because it had been moved at the last minute to an unfamiliar school auditorium, and she found herself trembling in the car park, unable to go in. Nisha said she wanted her life and her work back, but she was afraid that treatment might require her to stop being careful. More than anything, she hoped to find a way to be in public again without feeling that catastrophe was waiting just beyond the door.
